wstep: This card describes freezing fresh meat (game, lamb) according to the NCHFP, at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.

ostrzezenia.tekst: According to Clemson University (HGIC), do not rely on home freezing to destroy trichina: low temperatures kill trichina and other parasites only under very strict government-supervised conditions, and thorough cooking destroys all parasites.

akapity: Freeze only high-quality fresh meat.
Meat from the store can be frozen as is, or cut.
Cool home-slaughtered meat below 40 °F (about 4 °C) within 24 hours, best to 32–36 °F (about 0–2 °C), so it does not sour or spoil.
Variety meats such as liver, heart and sweetbreads are ready to wrap and freeze once cold.
Lamb is ready to cut and freeze after 24 hours of chilling.
Large game such as deer, moose or antelope is frozen like any other meat; trim and discard bloodshot meat before freezing.
Skin, dress and chill rabbit, squirrel and small game, then keep it in the refrigerator for 24–36 hours until the meat is no longer rigid; then cut it or leave it whole, package and freeze.
Package meat in meal-size portions and remove as many bones as possible.
Place two layers of freezer paper or wrap between slices or patties so they separate easily when frozen; this also speeds thawing.
Wrap meat in freezer paper or wrap using the drugstore or butcher wrap; ground meat, stew meat and small portions can be frozen in freezer bags or containers.
Over-wrap store-bought meat, because its clear packaging does not protect against moisture loss.
If it will stay in its original package longer than 2 months, overwrap it airtight with heavy-duty foil, plastic wrap or freezer paper, or place it in a bag.
Use packaging that is moisture- and vapor-resistant, durable and leakproof, and does not become brittle or crack in the cold.
Pack tightly, leaving as little air as possible, and press as much air as possible out of freezer bags before sealing.
Label each package with the name of the product, any added ingredients, the packaging date, the number of servings or amount, and the form, such as steaks or ground meat.
Freeze at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.
To speed up freezing, set the freezer to −10 °F (about −23 °C) or lower about 24 hours in advance.
Add to the freezer at one time only as much food as will freeze within 24 hours, because overloading slows freezing and lowers quality.
Spread new, warm packages with space between them, and stack them close together only once they are frozen.
According to Clemson University (HGIC), freeze as quickly as possible, because slow freezing forms large ice crystals that damage cells, and the meat loses juiciness when thawed.
According to the same source, a refrigerator freezing compartment that cannot hold 0 °F (−18 °C) or is opened often is for short-term storage only.
Keep the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, because at higher temperatures food loses quality faster; keep a freezer thermometer in it and check it often.
Freezing does not kill all bacteria, yeasts and molds; it only stops them multiplying while the food is held at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, and after thawing they can multiply again.
Food kept constantly at 0 °F (−18 °C) stays safe indefinitely, and the recommended storage times are for quality only: after them the food is still safe but lower in flavor, color and texture.
Freezer burn, grayish-brown leathery spots, is surface drying of poorly wrapped food caused by air; it does not make food unsafe, it only lowers quality, and the burned spots can be cut away.
For best quality, keep to the shorter time and use the oldest packages first.
According to the FDA, fresh lamb keeps its quality in the freezer for: steaks 6–12 months, chops 4–6 months, roasts 4–12 months, variety meats 3–4 months, ground and stew meat 3–4 months.
Thaw best in the refrigerator, in the original wrapping.
Faster: in waterproof wrapping in cold water that you change at least every 30 minutes so it stays cold.
Thaw in the microwave only if you will cook it immediately afterwards.
Never thaw on the kitchen counter, in a garage, basement, car or outdoors.

Thawing in the refrigerator needs planning: even a small amount of ground meat or boneless chicken breasts needs a full day, and a large item such as a turkey needs at least 1 day (24 hours) for every 5 pounds (about 2.3 kg).
Meat, fish and poultry can be cooked straight from the freezer, but extra time is needed, for large roasts up to 1 1/2 times as long.
For best quality, cook thawed meat or fish right away.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): refreeze without cooking only what thawed in the refrigerator, and put it back in the freezer within one to two days.
Cook anything you thawed in cold water or in the microwave first; only then may you freeze it.
Do not refreeze by any method anything that was in the danger zone for more than 2 hours (1 hour when the temperature is above 90 °F, about 32 °C); throw it out.
Do not keep perishable food out of the refrigerator for more than 2 hours, or for more than 1 hour when the temperature is above 90 °F (about 32 °C).
Food is safe while it stays frozen, but once it thaws and warms above 40 °F (about 4 °C), bacteria present before freezing can start to multiply.
During a power outage keep the freezer closed: according to the FDA, a full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, a half-full one for 24 hours.
According to the NCHFP, food stays frozen longer if the freezer is full, unopened, in a cool place and well insulated; it can be covered with blankets, away from the compressor.
JarAtlas rule (cautious) after a freezer failure: throw away any package that has no ice crystals and is above 40 °F (about 4 °C), or that you cannot check.
The FDA also says to throw away perishable food that has been at room temperature for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (about 32 °C) outside.
